OP from what I've read of your replies in here, it sounds like you got stuck in a shit high school. It sounds like you're having a bad time and you just want to get out of there. That's fair, it really is, but questioning whether high school is necessary is not going to fix the problem. If you drop out you will be a person without a high school education. It doesn't matter it you possess the knowledge or not, as far as anyone who doesn't know you is concerned, you don't have what it takes to make it through high school. It's harsh, I know, but think about this:

You're interviewing for a job, you submit your resume (which should have a detailed account of your educational background, everyone else applying will include that), and the employer sees that you didn't finish high school. Right away you're at a huge disadvantage relative to most (if not all) of the other applicants. The employer almost certainly went to high school and has a general idea of what it is you chose not to do. As you said somewhere else in here, high school is mostly regurgitation so it's not at all mentally challenging. This means that the employer knows right off the bat that you're either not intelligent enough to finish (and it sounds like that's not the case) or you couldn't get along with the other students. Either way that's a big red flag. The vast majority of jobs out there are looking for intelligent people who can play nice with others and your resume (sans a high school diploma or the equivalent) is screaming that you're missing one of those characteristics.

So to answer your question, yes, high school is absolutely necessary unless you want to play through life on the highest difficulty setting there is. Now if you want to talk about whether or not there's a better way to implement the educational system then I would agree we would be better off with a different one but I didn't get the impression that was the question you were asking.

You need money to get by. It sucks, but it's true. You don't have to make six figures, but you have to somehow consider it when you look for a job.

You also likely don't want to work 12 hours a day just to pay for rent and 2-3 meals a day. So you want a job that has a decent pay per hour, or is salaried with reasonable work hours.

Most of these jobs are somewhat specialized. In order to get that job, you need to prove that you can fill that specialization. Sometimes, this means spending the first 30 years of your life in school. Sometimes it means you have to go through a 3-week training course.

On the lower end of the spectrum, where the specialization is just a short training course, you need to prove to your employer that you are worth the time and money needed to send an employee through such a course. It's a lot easier to do this if you've graduated high school. On one hand, it shows that you have a decent general education. On another hand, it shows that you were capable of sticking with it until you finished (Employers don't want someone that has a history of bailing. And in your late teens/early 20s, high school is pretty much the only thing they can use to judge that).

A little higher on the spectrum, a high school education can get you into higher education. This doesn't always mean a 4-year college program. Trade school is a shorter program with better immediate payout. Associate's degrees at a local community college are way cheaper than 4-year state schools, and while they aren't as good as a bachelor's degree, they'll set you above someone with just a high school education. In some fields, you can take certification courses that allow you to perform jobs with more responsibility and more compensation.

And, although I mentioned it earlier in the post, I just want to reiterate: Employers want employees that will stick around. They want to see evidence that you will stick around. If they see that you dropped out of high school, the default "job" for every teenager in the country, they will think you're just gonna quit if the job gets too hard/you don't like it/too much drama with coworkers/whatever.
